title: A cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:6–8)

cards: Paul spent years running a collection. Churches of Gentile believers, in Greece and Asia Minor, were asked to put money aside for the poor believers in Jerusalem. He mentions it in Romans and in both letters to Corinth.
It was money, and it was also a sign: the newer churches sharing with the mother church that had given them the Gospel. In Second Corinthians he gives the subject a long stretch of the letter.
He praises the churches of Macedonia, who gave out of deep poverty, beyond their means. Then he turns to Corinth, which had promised a lot and not yet delivered.

teach.b: He starts with a farmer's rule: whoever sows sparingly will reap sparingly, and whoever sows generously will reap generously.
Then he says how to give: "Every one as he hath determined in his heart, not with sadness, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
First, decide in your heart. Paul doesn't set an amount.
Second, not with sadness: no grudging, no giving while silently resenting it. Third, not of necessity: not squeezed out by pressure or shame.
The Greek word for cheerful is hilaros: glad, bright, ready.
Paul seems to be echoing a line from the old Greek version of the book of Proverbs, which says God blesses a cheerful giver.
Then he adds a promise: God is able to make all grace abound in you, so that you have enough, and enough left over for every good work. In Paul's picture, giving isn't a loss to be endured.
It's seed, and God keeps you supplied with more. Catholics put this into practice in many ways. Almsgiving is one of the three traditional practices of Lent, with prayer and fasting.
The Catechism counts giving to the poor among the works of mercy and calls it a work of justice pleasing to God. But Paul's interest here is less in the amount than in the face.
Two people can put the same money in the basket. One with a sigh. One with a smile.
Paul says God loves the second.

how: Catholics give through the parish collection at Mass, through Lenten almsgiving, and through charities such as the Society of St. Vincent de Paul; the Church counts almsgiving among the works of mercy.

o: generous with money, whatever the mood
glad, bright and ready, giving without a sigh
loud and laughing, the life of the party

games.q: you're in Corinth, and Paul's letter asks for your share of the collection. how does he want you to give?
o: to match Macedonia, so Corinth isn't shamed.
as you've decided in your heart, gladly.
a set amount, enforced by the elders.
games.why: "every one as he hath determined in his heart, not with sadness, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."

practice: Think of one small thing you could give: money to someone who needs it, your time, a meal, ten minutes of your full attention.
Make it small enough to give without a sigh, decide it in your heart now so it isn't squeezed out of you later, and picture your face as you give it.
If you pray, offer the gift to God first; if not, just decide, and let yourself be glad about it.

wordCard.voice: Hilaros. Greek for glad, bright, ready: the kind of giving God loves, decided in the heart, not squeezed out by sadness or pressure. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: cheerful. A gift decided in the heart, not squeezed out. Until next time.
